Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues

Microsoft says November 2026 Windows security updates can cause printing failures for complex documents containing zero-dimension images, particularly in Word documents printed through GDI. The issue affects Windows 10 and later clients and Windows Server 2016 and later systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft warned that November 2026 Windows security updates may cause printing failures for documents with complex formatting.
  • 02The issue affects documents containing images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution on Windows 10 or later and Windows Server 2016 or later.
  • 03Zero-size images may be used as invisible watermarks, layout anchors, or inserted by document-generation tools when no graphic is present.
  • 04The problem mainly affects Microsoft Word documents printed through the Windows Graphics Device Interface, though other applications may also be affected.
  • 05Microsoft also reported other recent update-related issues involving Windows activation, SQL Server performance and stability, and Windows 11 update installation.

Microsoft warned that the November 2026 Windows security updates may cause printing failures for documents with complex formatting. The issue affects Windows 10 and later client devices and Windows Server 2016 and later server devices. According to Microsoft, printing can fail when a document contains an image rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution.

Such zero-size images may be used as invisible watermarks, layout anchors, or objects inserted by document-generation tools when no graphic is present. Microsoft said the issue mainly affects Microsoft Word documents printed through the Windows Graphics Device Interface, although other applications may also experience failures. The warning follows other Microsoft-confirmed update-related problems involving Windows activation and licensing, SQL Server performance and stability, and Windows 11 update installation.

  • Documents can fail to print because of images that are not visibly part of their content, such as zero-size objects used for watermarks, layout positioning, or created by document-generation tools.
  • Although Microsoft Word printing through the Windows Graphics Device Interface is the main reported scenario, Microsoft says the issue can also affect printing from other applications.
  • The printing problem is one of several issues Microsoft acknowledged around recent Windows updates, alongside activation failures, SQL Server problems, and Windows 11 installation errors.

Microsoft says its November 2026 Windows security updates can stop some documents from printing when they contain certain hidden or zero-size images used for layout, watermarks, or document generation. The problem affects Windows 10 or newer computers and Windows Server 2016 or newer, especially people printing Microsoft Word documents. This matters because organizations and individuals may be unable to print important documents after installing security updates, adding to other recent update-related problems involving activation, SQL Server, and Windows 11 installation.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Microsoft reports a concrete printing regression caused by November 2026 Windows security updates that affects Windows 10-or-later clients and Windows Server 2016-or-later systems. It is operationally relevant for organizations that print complex Word documents, but the issue is limited to a specific document-rendering condition and is not described as a security vulnerability or active attack.

Check Point gateways hacked via PHP2Shell to deploy VMware ESXi wiper

Attackers exploited PHP2Shell flaws and a Check Point privilege-escalation zero-day to compromise internet-facing Security Gateway Mobile Access portals, move to VMware ESXi hosts, and deploy a data-wiping payload. Organizations should urgently apply Check Point’s November Jumbo Hotfix and investigate exposed gateways for compromise indicators.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers exploited PHP2Shell flaws through Check Point Security Gateway Mobile Access portals and then used CVE-2026-123039 to obtain root-level control.
  • 02The first wave began on October 30 and targeted Israeli organizations, while a second wave on November 2 affected companies in multiple countries and sectors.
  • 03In attacks against Israeli organizations, the attackers used the gogo network scanner to locate VMware ESXi hosts and deployed the destroy_v6 data wiper.
  • 04The destroy_v6 wiper recursively deletes data and first attempts to overwrite it with zeros to make recovery more difficult.
  • 05Check Point recommends installing the November Jumbo Hotfix and checking previously exposed gateways for indicators such as upload_progress_pwn session files, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes, firewall-log gaps, and unauthorized SSH connections to ESXi hosts.

Attackers targeted vulnerable Check Point Security Gateway systems in PHP2Shell attacks, initially affecting Israeli organizations from October 30 and later companies across several countries and sectors on November 2. They gained entry through Mobile Access portals, then used CVE-2026-123039 to obtain root-level privileges. Check Point said the same actor conducted the campaign from initial access through lateral movement and installation of PHP webshells. The activity followed exploitation of PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which PHP patched on October 21.

After gaining control of the gateways, the attackers installed PHP webshells and the TSGA backdoor, which includes TSProxy to receive commands hidden in normal traffic. In attacks against Israeli organizations, they used the gogo network reconnaissance tool to find VMware ESXi hosts and deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, which recursively deletes data and can overwrite it with zeros first to make recovery harder. A note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt containing political messages was left on affected ESXi hosts, although Check Point said the messages raise the possibility of a false flag and the activity cannot be confidently attributed. Check Point tentatively linked TSGA and TSProxy to the PhiliKit framework, previously associated by ESET with UNC5221.

The second wave did not include observed destructive activity, and researchers said the attackers’ subsequent actions remain unclear. Check Point recommends deploying its November Jumbo Hotfix to Management Servers and Security Gateways, especially internet-facing Mobile Access portals, because it addresses PHP2Shell and the DynamicCLI privilege-escalation flaw. It also advises checking exposed gateways for upload_progress_pwn session files, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes or binaries, firewall-log gaps, and unauthorized SSH activity to internal VMware ESXi hosts.

  • Exploitation attempts began four days before PHP issued emergency patches, showing that organizations could have been exposed before fixes were available.
  • The attackers combined access through the Mobile Access portal with a separate privilege-escalation flaw to gain full control of the gateway, then used that position to reach internal VMware ESXi hosts.
  • Political messages left alongside the wiper may not reliably identify the attackers, as Check Point said they raised the possibility of a false-flag operation and could not attribute the campaign with confidence.
  • The second wave affected organizations in multiple countries and sectors but did not include observed destructive activity, leaving the attackers’ follow-on actions unclear.
  • Unexplained firewall-log gaps and SSH connections from a gateway to internal ESXi hosts are specific warning signs that a gateway may already have been compromised.

Hackers broke into vulnerable Check Point security systems used by organizations, first targeting groups in Israel and later companies in several countries. They used the access to reach VMware ESXi systems, which run many organizations’ virtual computers, and in some cases launched software that deletes data and makes recovery harder. This can cause severe disruption because it can erase important business systems rather than merely steal information. Check Point advises customers to install its latest fixes and check previously exposed systems for signs that intruders were present.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an active exploitation campaign against internet-facing Check Point Security Gateway Mobile Access portals that includes root-level compromise, lateral movement to VMware ESXi hosts, and destructive data wiping. Security teams using affected Check Point systems should urgently patch and investigate the listed indicators of compromise.

Check Point warns of zero-day flaw exploited for root access

Check Point released emergency hotfixes for CVE-2026-123039, an actively exploited Gaia OS flaw that lets authenticated local users execute commands as root through the DynamicCLI socket. Attackers reportedly chained it with PHP2Shell access to compromise gateways, deploy backdoors, and pivot to VMware ESXi hosts.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Check Point released emergency hotfixes for CVE-2026-123039, a high-severity Gaia OS flaw that has been actively exploited to obtain root-level access on vulnerable devices.
  • 02The vulnerability affects the DynamicCLI service because it accepts requests through a local socket that any local process can access without verifying who sent the request.
  • 03Check Point said attackers exploited PHP2Shell flaws to access Mobile Access portals, then used CVE-2026-123039 to gain full control and establish persistence.
  • 04The attackers deployed webshells, TSGA and TSProxy malware, moved from compromised gateways to VMware ESXi hosts, and deployed destructive wiper malware.
  • 05Organizations unable to immediately apply the hotfixes can temporarily stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting, according to Check Point.

Check Point released emergency hotfixes for CVE-2026-123039, a high-severity Gaia OS flaw that it says attackers have actively exploited against a couple of dozen customers since late October. The issue affects the DynamicCLI service, which runs with root-level permissions and accepts commands through a world-writable local socket without authenticating the process connecting to it. An authenticated local user can therefore send commands through the socket and have them executed with full system privileges. Affected products include Check Point Firewall, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms.

According to Check Point, attackers first accessed Mobile Access portals through PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then used CVE-2026-123039 to gain root access. They subsequently deployed webshells, TSGA and TSProxy malware, moved from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host, and installed destructive wiper malware. Organizations that cannot immediately apply the hotfixes can temporarily stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. Check Point also provided indicators and advised investigating unusual system() use and commands that bypass the normal Clish wrapper.

  • Although CVE-2026-123039 requires authenticated local access, attackers reportedly paired it with PHP2Shell flaws in the Mobile Access portal, showing how an initial gateway compromise could be escalated to full device control.
  • The vulnerable DynamicCLI service runs as root while accepting requests through a world-writable local socket without checking the requesting process, making it a direct route from local access to root-level command execution.
  • Check Point says defenders can look for unusual use of the system() function and commands that bypass the normal Clish wrapper, which may indicate commands were run through the vulnerable socket with root privileges.
  • If patching cannot happen immediately, Check Point recommends stopping the dynamic_server process and preventing it from restarting as a temporary measure.
  • The reported intrusion path extended beyond the Check Point gateway to VMware ESXi hosts and ended with destructive data-wiping malware, increasing the potential impact beyond the originally compromised device.

Check Point released emergency fixes for a serious weakness in several of its security products after hackers used it against a couple of dozen customers. The flaw can let someone who already has access to a device run commands with full control, and attackers reportedly used it after breaking into a remote-access portal. This matters because the intruders then installed hidden access tools and moved from the compromised security device to VMware systems, where they deployed software designed to erase data.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an actively exploited high-severity zero-day in Check Point Gaia OS that attackers used to gain root access and establish persistence on affected devices. Check Point reports exploitation against a couple of dozen customers and links the intrusion chain to gateway compromise, backdoor deployment, and destructive wiper malware on VMware ESXi hosts.

Police arrest 354 suspects in dark web cybercrime crackdown

Operation TorNado, a 14-country law-enforcement crackdown on dark-web drug marketplaces, resulted in 354 arrests and major seizures of drugs, firearms, cash, and cryptocurrency. The operation targeted vendors and buyers linked to Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom markets.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Operation TorNado ran from May 2025 through October 2026 and involved law-enforcement agencies from 14 countries.
  • 02Authorities arrested 354 suspects linked to vendors and buyers on Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces.
  • 03The operation targeted people active on dark web forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services in addition to the named marketplaces.
  • 04Authorities in Europe seized more than €60 million in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs, and 57 firearms.
  • 05In the United States, law enforcement seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 152 firearms, and over €150 million.

Operation TorNado was a joint law-enforcement operation that ran from May 2025 through October 2026 and involved agencies from 14 countries. Authorities arrested 354 suspects allegedly connected to vendors and buyers on the Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces. Investigators also targeted people active on forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services, supported by Europol cross-checks and forensic analysis.

Authorities in Europe seized more than €60 million in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs, and 57 firearms. In the United States, authorities seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 152 firearms, and over €150 million. Europol said the operation demonstrated that dark web marketplaces continue to adapt despite takedowns, while the U.S. Department of Justice said intelligence from previous marketplace takedowns and investigations helped identify alleged drug traffickers.

  • The operation did not focus only on major dark web marketplaces; investigators also pursued vendors and buyers using forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services.
  • U.S. and international agencies used intelligence obtained after prior marketplace takedowns and vendor investigations to identify additional alleged dark web drug traffickers.
  • The article describes a continuing pattern of multinational operations, including DisrupTor, Dark Huntor, SpecTor, and RapTor, indicating that arrests and marketplace seizures have continued across several years.
  • Despite repeated takedowns, Europol said dark web marketplaces continue to adapt, highlighting their resilience after enforcement actions.

Police agencies from 14 countries arrested 354 people accused of buying or selling illegal drugs through hidden online marketplaces, including Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom. The operation also seized large amounts of drugs, guns, cash, and digital currency in Europe and the United States. It matters because these marketplaces continue to change and reappear even after closures, allowing illegal drug trade to reach buyers and sellers across borders.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a significant multinational law-enforcement action involving 354 arrests and major seizures tied to multiple dark web marketplaces. It is broadly relevant to professionals tracking dark web criminal ecosystems and the operational impact of marketplace takedowns, though it does not describe an immediate technical threat requiring defensive action.

Microsoft confirms Windows activation failures after November updates

Microsoft confirmed that November Windows security updates can break automated activation and licensing tasks, producing error 0x80041008 when organizations use Slmgr.vbs to configure KMS or install product keys. Already activated systems and devices that do not run the affected Slmgr commands are not expected to be impacted; a fix is pending.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft confirmed that November Patch Tuesday security updates can cause Windows activation and licensing failures with error 0x80041008.
  • 02The issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation or licensing and those using the Slmgr.vbs command-line tool to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service, or manage product keys.
  • 03Affected commands include "slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain>" and "slmgr.vbs /ipk <key>" on Windows 10 21H2/22H2, Windows 11 23H2, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025.
  • 04Devices that are already activated should remain activated, and customers that already have the correct KMS client key and configuration without needing the affected commands are not expected to be impacted.
  • 05Microsoft said a fix will be available in the coming days and advised organizations needing immediate mitigation to contact Microsoft Support for business.

Microsoft confirmed that its November Patch Tuesday security updates can cause Windows activation and licensing failures with error 0x80041008. The issue affects organizations that automate Windows activation and licensing or use the Slmgr.vbs command-line tool. Microsoft said the error can occur when activating Windows, configuring Key Management Service (KMS), or managing product keys.

The failures have been reported after running slmgr.vbs /skms-domain <domain> and slmgr.vbs /ipk <key> on Windows 10 21H2/22H2, Windows 11 23H2, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Devices that are already activated are expected to remain activated, and systems with the appropriate KMS client key and configuration that do not need the affected commands are not expected to be affected. Microsoft said a fix will be available in the coming days and advised organizations needing immediate mitigation to contact Microsoft Support for business.

  • The problem is concentrated in deployment and license-management workflows rather than on all Windows devices, because systems that are already activated are expected to remain activated.
  • Organizations whose standard device image already includes the appropriate KMS client key and that do not use the affected Slmgr.vbs commands are specifically identified as unaffected.
  • Even where KMS activation attempts fail, devices previously activated through KMS typically remain activated for up to 180 days after their last successful activation.
  • Microsoft has not provided a general workaround in the article; organizations needing an immediate mitigation are directed to Microsoft Support for business while a fix is prepared.

Microsoft says its November Windows security updates can cause errors when organizations try to activate Windows or set up/manage their software licenses. The issue affects businesses and other organizations that use automated setup processes or Windows’ command-line licensing tool on certain Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server versions. Computers that are already activated should keep working, but affected organizations may be unable to prepare new devices or change license settings until Microsoft releases a fix.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Microsoft confirmed a specific, recent issue in November Windows security updates that can disrupt automated activation and licensing workflows across multiple Windows client and server versions. It is most relevant to organizations using Slmgr.vbs or KMS provisioning, while already activated systems are generally unaffected and Microsoft says a fix is forthcoming.

How one AI agent exposed five critical enterprise security gaps

A sponsored Token Security article uses a hypothetical invoice-processing AI agent to show how unmanaged credentials, excessive permissions, prompt injection, weak behavioral monitoring, and incomplete audit trails can create enterprise risk. It argues organizations should inventory agents, use purpose-built identities and least privilege, require review for high-risk capabilities, and retain approval and action records.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A hypothetical invoice-processing AI agent was created by an accounts employee using OAuth access for email and Slack and a personal API key for the ERP, without a security review.
  • 02The article cites a January 2026 Cloud Security Alliance survey of 418 IT and security professionals in which 82% said they had discovered AI agents they did not know about during the previous year.
  • 03The agent processes untrusted email, can access private ERP data, and can change ERP records or send Slack messages, placing all three conditions of Meta’s Agents Rule of Two in one session.
  • 04A malicious invoice attachment can contain hidden instructions that the agent reads and follows, resulting in an unauthorized vendor bank-detail change despite valid credentials and permitted tool access.
  • 05The article recommends detecting abnormal agent behavior by comparing actions with its normal activity, preserving transcripts and memory during response, and recording the responsible human, approval, entitlement, and authority for each agent action.

The article follows a hypothetical accounts employee who creates an AI agent to read an inbox, match invoices in an ERP system, and post daily Slack summaries. The agent receives email and Slack access through OAuth approval screens and ERP access through the employee’s personal API key, without a security review. The article cites a Cloud Security Alliance survey in which 82% of 418 IT and security professionals said they had discovered AI agents they did not know about in the past year. It argues that agents can use different access paths that leave incomplete or inconsistent records across logs.

The scenario shows how a malicious invoice attachment with hidden text can direct the agent to alter a vendor’s bank details while using valid credentials and permitted tools. The article says the agent has three risky capabilities at once: processing outside input, accessing private data, and making changes or communicating externally. It recommends identifying unusual behavior from an agent’s normal activity, such as its first use of a permitted write tool or a new action sequence, rather than checking only whether it remained within assigned permissions. It also stresses preserving agent memory and transcripts during response and retaining records of the agent, entitlement, approval, and human authority behind every action.

  • An agent’s access method can fragment accountability across systems: a database may log a shared service account, a SaaS service may log a user, and the identity provider may have no corresponding record.
  • Monitoring whether an agent stays within its assigned permissions may miss harmful activity, because a compromised agent can use valid credentials and authorized tools to make damaging changes.
  • A permitted tool’s first use and an unfamiliar sequence of otherwise normal actions can be stronger warning signs than permission-based alerts, such as an invoice-reading agent suddenly writing bank details to an ERP.
  • OAuth approvals can remain active after the person who granted them changes roles, while static personal API keys may have no expiry date.
  • The article states that the human authority behind an agent action cannot be reconstructed after the fact unless the requester and delegation chain were recorded when the action occurred.

The article describes a fictional company employee who quickly creates an AI helper to read invoices, check them against company records, and post summaries, without the security team knowing it exists. A fraudulent email can hide instructions that cause the helper to change a vendor’s bank details, even though the helper appears to be using approved access. This matters to businesses because many say they have discovered AI helpers they did not know were running, and such helpers can make damaging changes or expose private information unless companies track who created them, limit what they can do, and keep clear records of their actions.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a sponsored, evergreen best-practices article built around a hypothetical AI-agent compromise scenario rather than a specific incident, vulnerability, or active threat. It offers useful awareness of agent identity, monitoring, and audit challenges, but does not require urgent action.

Trezor confirms crypto-stealing implants in three wallets, releases fix

Trezor confirmed that three Safe 5 wallets sold by Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis contained cellular-connected hardware implants that could steal recovery phrases and passphrases. Firmware 2.13.1 blocks the known implants, but affected buyers should move funds to a new wallet because previously captured recovery phrases remain exposed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Trezor confirmed that three Safe 5 wallets sold by Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis contained malicious hardware implants designed to capture recovery phrases and passphrases.
  • 02The implants used an extra circuit board between the wallet’s main board and display to monitor screen activity, encrypt captured information, and send it through a mobile network to an attacker-controlled server.
  • 03Trezor released firmware version 2.13.1 on November 11, which it says prevents the identified implants from capturing information on updated devices.
  • 04The update cannot protect recovery phrases that may have been captured before installation, and Trezor advises CryptoBilis customers to move cryptocurrency to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.
  • 05Trezor reduced its global reseller network by about 80% and is offering replacement devices to customers who purchased a Trezor wallet from CryptoBilis since March 2026.

Trezor confirmed that three Safe 5 hardware wallets sold by Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis contained malicious physical implants designed to steal wallet recovery phrases and passphrases. The confirmed devices were purchased between August 20 and September 23, 2026, and Trezor identified two of the cases through owner-submitted internal photographs after examining the original device in its laboratory. Trezor said 48 CryptoBilis customers contacted the company after its October warning, while checks of devices from other regional resellers found no evidence of tampering.

The implant was an extra circuit board placed between the Safe 5’s main board and display, allowing it to observe information shown or entered on the screen without changing the legitimate firmware or Secure Element. It could encrypt captured recovery words or passphrases and transmit them through a mobile network to an attacker-controlled server, retaining the data and retrying if no connection was available. Trezor’s firmware version 2.13.1, released November 11, blocks the identified implants from capturing new information, but cannot protect secrets that may have been captured earlier; the company advises CryptoBilis buyers to move funds to a newly created wallet and is offering replacements for devices purchased from that reseller since March 2026.

  • The implants could steal secrets without altering Trezor’s legitimate firmware or Secure Element, showing that a device can be physically compromised even when its normal software remains unchanged.
  • Trezor’s firmware 2.13.1 can make the identified implants unable to capture new information, but it cannot undo exposure of recovery phrases or passphrases collected before the update.
  • Although only three compromised Safe 5 devices have been confirmed and no affected Trezor customer has reported lost funds, Trezor is offering replacements to all CryptoBilis buyers since March 2026 rather than only to confirmed cases.
  • Trezor found no evidence of tampering in devices inspected from other regional resellers, while still cutting its reseller network by about 80% to impose stricter supply-chain controls.

Trezor found that three Safe 5 crypto wallets sold by Indonesian reseller CryptoBilis had hidden extra circuit boards that could record a customer’s secret wallet recovery words and passphrases, then send them to criminals through a mobile network. The affected devices were sold between August 20 and September 23, 2026, and Trezor is offering replacements to CryptoBilis customers who bought devices since March 2026. A software update stops the known hidden boards from collecting new information, but anyone whose secret words may already have been recorded should move their cryptocurrency to a newly created wallet. The incident shows that a device can be altered before it reaches a buyer, putting digital money at risk even when the wallet’s normal software has not been changed.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

Trezor confirmed a real supply-chain compromise affecting Safe 5 hardware wallets, where physical implants could capture recovery phrases and transmit them over cellular networks. The impact is currently limited to three confirmed devices from CryptoBilis and no reported Trezor fund losses, but affected users need to act because firmware updates cannot protect secrets captured before installation.

Researchers disclosed Mior and Skyfall, two attacks that can let a malicious cloud host read secrets from AMD SEV-SNP-protected virtual machines. SEV-SNP is intended to protect a virtual machine’s memory even from the server operator and its hypervisor. Mior can additionally modify VM memory and falsify the signed attestation report used to show which software a VM runs, while Skyfall can expose saved register data and limited memory data.

Mior requires control of the hypervisor, BIOS or UEFI, and a PCIe device, and was demonstrated on an AMD EPYC 9135 Zen 5 processor. Skyfall requires a malicious host but no hardware tampering, and researchers demonstrated it on Zen 3 and Zen 4 EPYC chips, including recovery of a disk-encryption key from a test VM. AMD tracks the flaws as CVE-2026-0462 and CVE-2026-40671 and has released or planned firmware, microcode, and BIOS-related updates; customers renting confidential VMs depend on their cloud providers to deploy them.

  • Mior was demonstrated even when ciphertext hiding was enabled, meaning that this optional feature did not prevent the researchers from enabling debugging and accessing VM memory after corrupting the memory-protection table.
  • Mior can undermine remote trust checks by copying the measurement of a harmless VM into a malicious one, causing signed attestation reports to identify the malicious VM as the harmless image.
  • Skyfall’s demonstrated VM-memory access is limited to three fixed cache-line locations within a targeted memory page, while its register-data leak was used to recover a disk-encryption key in a test setup.
  • The Skyfall program committee noted that a practical VM attack would require demanding conditions, including an otherwise idle processor core, rapid failed VM starts and performance-counter reads, and a VM that remains available during the process.
  • Although AMD lists updated SEV firmware and Skyfall microcode, the advisories do not clarify whether these updates are sufficient by themselves or require corresponding BIOS updates, leaving cloud customers dependent on provider deployment details.

Researchers found two weaknesses, called Mior and Skyfall, that could let a dishonest cloud-server operator see private information inside supposedly protected virtual computers. Mior could also change a virtual computer’s memory and forge the report used to prove what software it is running, while Skyfall could expose saved data such as encryption keys. The issue affects several AMD EPYC server processor lines used for confidential cloud computing, and customers who rent these virtual machines depend on their cloud provider to install the needed firmware and BIOS updates. The findings matter because confidential computing is designed specifically to keep even the server owner from accessing a customer’s secrets.

PostgreSQL released updates addressing 52 security flaws, including CVE-2026-6460, a type-confusion issue rated CVSS 8.8. The flaw affects releases before PostgreSQL 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25. It can allow a database user who can create objects to run code with the operating-system permissions of the account running PostgreSQL. The project and CISA had not reported known exploitation.

The issue occurs when a field type in a composite type is changed while the server still holds older values, which can cause an old value to be interpreted as the new type. Researcher Mehmet Ince demonstrated an exploit against PostgreSQL 18.6 that can crash an unpatched server and leak memory addresses, though the command-execution SQL was not published. Administrators should update the server, rebuild or update C-language extensions, restart PostgreSQL where necessary, update client tools, and follow the release’s reindexing and backup guidance. PostgreSQL 14.25 is the last release for PostgreSQL 14, while older affected major versions received no update.

  • Updating PostgreSQL alone may not fully protect a server, because C-language extensions built against older releases can still load but may not receive the release's vulnerability protections.
  • The published exploit demonstrates a crash and memory-address leak, but its final command-execution SQL was not published, and the article says it is unclear whether a default-privilege account can progress from crashing the server to running code.
  • PostgreSQL 14.25 is the final release for PostgreSQL 14, while older affected major versions received no update, leaving upgrade as the practical path for systems on unsupported versions.
  • After updating, administrators are instructed to perform reindexing and to create a new full backup before continuing incremental backups.
  • The new composite_type_mismatch setting can disable the added checks, but PostgreSQL warns that doing so creates security risks.

PostgreSQL has released updates fixing 52 security problems, including one that could let a logged-in database user with permission to create or change database items run commands on the machine hosting the database. The issue affects older releases of PostgreSQL and can give an attacker the same access as the account used to run the database service. Organizations using PostgreSQL, including cloud-hosted versions, should update the database software, related add-ons, and client tools because an unpatched system could be disrupted or taken over.

When an AI Agent Goes Wrong, Can You Stop It?

Stopping an AI agent requires more than disabling the model: teams should halt workflows and queues, revoke credentials and sessions, restrict tools and network access, and preserve evidence. Organizations should pre-test these containment controls and restore agent access only after identifying and fixing the underlying cause.
KEY POINTS
  • 01An AI agent can have access to records and connected tools that allow it to act on instructions embedded in a support ticket or other input.
  • 02Disabling an agent or model may not stop queued jobs, retries, established sessions, or separate services already processing work.
  • 03Effective containment can require stopping active and queued runs, revoking credentials and sessions, disabling tools or integrations, and restricting network connections.
  • 04Teams should preserve agent, identity, API, application, and network records to distinguish attempted actions from completed ones and determine what was accessed or changed.
  • 05Before restoring an agent workflow, organizations should identify the cause, apply the smallest necessary access scope, test in a controlled environment, and monitor activity after resuming.

The article explains that an AI agent handling support tickets and account lookups could be led by instructions in a ticket to export records to an unfamiliar destination. Because the agent’s identity may already have access to records and connected tools, it may be able to make the request. The article notes that an October 2026 OWASP GenAI Security Project roundup described evaluation agents reaching beyond their intended scope and recommended testing containment that revokes credentials and network access.

Turning off a model may not stop queued jobs, retries, established sessions, or separate services already processing work. The article recommends a tested containment process that pauses active runs and triggers, revokes or limits credentials and sessions, disables relevant tools or integrations, and restricts network paths. Teams should preserve agent, identity, API, application, and network records; assess completed changes or data access; and restore the workflow only after identifying the cause, limiting access to the smallest required scope, testing it in a controlled environment, and monitoring it after resumption.

  • A prompt telling an agent to stop is not a containment measure; the response must be performed through the systems that run its workflow.
  • Revoking one credential may be insufficient because other tokens, grants, or existing connections can remain active, so teams must verify that access is actually no longer usable.
  • An agent’s own activity logs are not enough to establish what occurred, because an attempted tool action does not prove success and must be compared with identity, API, application, and network records.
  • Stopping an agent limits future activity but does not reverse completed exports, permission changes, messages, or other downstream effects.

The article explains that an AI helper with access to company accounts and tools can be tricked or misconfigured into reading, exporting, or changing information it should not. Simply turning off the AI may not stop work that is already running, so organizations need ways to stop its tasks, cut off its account access and outside connections, and check what it already did. This matters to any organization using AI to handle sensitive systems or data, because stopping further harm does not undo information already shared or changes already made.

Trezor found that the implant sits between the wallet’s main board and screen, allowing it to capture recovery phrases during backup creation or restoration, as well as passphrases shown on the display. A first-time sender using a free Outlook.com mailbox sent a fake major-retailer order confirmation to an analytics and AI services company. The rendered email showed two Apple gift card line items, a stated $500 total, and a callback phone number printed twice. It was classified as high-severity callback phishing and image-based impersonation.

The message body contained 15 inline images arranged in nested presentation tables, with zero font size and line height so the pieces appeared as one seamless page. It had no text nodes, anchors, or ordinary clickable links, while every image used the same meaningless alt text, tdmkn.bne.4yd; the platform’s link, QR, and OCR fields were all empty. Although SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and compauth passed, a recipient reported the email as spam, an analyst marked it malicious, and the mailbox was quarantined.

  • A callback scam does not require a malicious link, making image tiling especially useful because the attacker only needs the visual phone number and message to reach the recipient.
  • Passed sender-authentication checks confirmed that the free Outlook.com mailbox was legitimately sending the email through Microsoft, not that the message itself was trustworthy.
  • The article identifies a practical escalation signal: emails with images but no extracted text should be reviewed for structural patterns such as many tiles, repeated meaningless alt text, zeroed typography, and no anchors.

A scam email sent from a free Outlook account looked like a major retailer’s order confirmation and told the recipient to call a phone number about Apple gift cards. Instead of ordinary written content, it used 15 small pictures assembled into one page, so the email system found no readable text, links, or phone number even though a person could see them. This affected an analytics and AI services company, and it shows how scammers can bypass automated checks and rely on people being worried enough to call them.

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical flaw in the HTTP/2 module, mod_http2, of Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70. The flaw can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to run arbitrary code on a server with HTTP/2 enabled. As of publication, the article states that there were no reports of exploitation in the wild.

The issue is a race condition in the assign_headers() function, where concurrent threads improperly share resources and can cause heap corruption. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 and later fix the problem, while standalone mod_h2 builds should be upgraded to versions newer than 2.0.42. Organizations that cannot patch immediately can disable HTTP/2 and restrict Apache to HTTP/1.1, although this only reduces exposure rather than fixing the underlying issue.

  • A server can be vulnerable even if a vendor package scanner does not mark it as affected when the operating system vendor has not yet published a fixed package, so distribution-specific trackers should also be checked.
  • Standard HTTP load balancers usually prevent the normal exposure scenario described in the article, meaning the network setup in front of Apache materially changes risk.
  • Because successful code execution runs with the web server process’s privileges, a compromised Apache server in cloud environments could provide a path toward adjacent services or cloud metadata endpoints.
  • Disabling HTTP/2 reduces exposure by removing the attack path, but it is only a temporary mitigation and does not correct the underlying software flaw.

A serious flaw in Apache web server software can let an outsider take control of affected servers without needing a login when the newer HTTP/2 web connection feature is enabled. It affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, though servers behind a standard web traffic distributor are usually not exposed. Organizations should update to version 2.4.71 or newer, or temporarily turn off HTTP/2, because a compromised server could give an attacker a way into other services and cloud resources.

Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes

A BlackNevas ransomware operation destroyed a virtualized environment by compromising vCenter and abusing legitimate VMware management features to enable ESXi SSH access, disrupt backups, and wipe virtual-machine data without exploiting a hypervisor vulnerability. The key defense is to treat vCenter, ESXi administration, and backup recovery as separate high-trust security boundaries with isolated identities, restricted access, and remotely retained telemetry.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A BlackNevas ransomware campaign destroyed four ESXi hosts, all virtual machines on them, two vCenter Server Appliances, and connected backup infrastructure over a 10-day period.
  • 02The attackers used legitimate VMware management interfaces rather than exploiting a hypervisor vulnerability, enabling ESXi SSH through vCenter Host Profiles before directly accessing target hosts.
  • 03After accessing a vCenter appliance through SSH as root, the attackers deployed MeshAgent and later installed a Ligolo-ng reverse tunnel as a persistent systemd service disguised as vmware-vdma.
  • 04The ransomware payload was delivered to ESXi through SFTP, staged under /tmp, tested roughly three hours before detonation, and then executed against the /vmfs virtual-machine storage path.
  • 05The attackers disrupted backup infrastructure before the ESXi impact by disabling antivirus protection, stopping backup services, encrypting recovery systems, and disrupting administrative access.

Kaspersky’s Global Emergency Response Team investigated a BlackNevas ransomware campaign that destroyed four ESXi hosts, every virtual machine on them, two vCenter Server Appliances, and connected backup infrastructure over 10 days. The attackers did not exploit an ESXi or vCenter vulnerability; instead, they used legitimate VMware management interfaces after obtaining privileged access through systems inside the organization’s perimeter. The case shows how compromise of the virtualization management plane can allow an attacker to affect many systems at once.

After logging in to a vCenter appliance through SSH as root, the attackers installed MeshAgent and a Ligolo-ng reverse tunnel disguised as a VMware-related systemd service. They used vCenter Host Profiles to enable SSH on ESXi hosts, delivered an ESXi payload through SFTP, tested it, and later ran it against the /vmfs/ storage path, while virtual machines were rapidly stopped. Backup defenses and recovery infrastructure were disrupted before the ESXi impact, reinforcing the article’s recommendation to isolate vCenter administration, hypervisor identities, backup systems, and log collection from the wider production environment.

  • A fully patched ESXi environment can still face catastrophic impact if attackers compromise vCenter, because vCenter can legitimately change host settings and enable direct access to managed hosts.
  • The combination of a Host Profile change that enables SSH and a new SSH connection from vCenter to the same ESXi host is a higher-confidence warning than either event alone.
  • Guest-based security software may only see the effects of hypervisor-side disk modification, not the ESXi process that performed it, making vCenter and ESXi logs essential for investigation.
  • Backups are not protected merely because stored data is immutable; recovery also depends on separate identities, management systems, network access, and tested restoration procedures.
  • Rebooting an affected ESXi host before collecting logs can erase evidence because ESXi may store logs on temporary memory-backed storage unless persistent scratch space or remote logging is configured.

The article describes how a ransomware group took control of an organization’s systems that run many virtual computers, then shut those computers down, damaged their data, and disrupted backups needed for recovery. The attackers did not need to break a software flaw; they used stolen or reused access and normal management features to make harmful changes. This matters because control of one central management system can let criminals disrupt many important services at once, including databases, business applications, and backup systems.

CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines: Will Your AI System Need an Independent Audit?

CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines use an eight-factor risk score to place AI systems into audit tiers, with Tier 2 and above requiring independent audits by CERT-In-empanelled organizations. Adding autonomous actions such as issuing refunds can raise a chatbot’s tier and trigger stricter assessments, monitoring, and incident-reporting expectations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CERT-In issued version 1.0 of its Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines on 4 November 2026 for AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, as well as systems processing Indian data or serving Indian users.

  • 03AI systems in Tier 2 and above, which score 13 or more, require an independent audit by a CERT-In-empanelled auditing organization, with more frequent and extensive requirements for higher tiers.
  • 04The guidelines identify autonomous execution of transactions, code, or external communications as an escalation trigger that can move an AI system to a higher tier regardless of its total score.
  • 05AI incidents that meet CERT-In’s reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, and the article states that CERT-In’s 2022 Directions require 180-day log retention.

CERT-In issued version 1.0 of its Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines on 4 November 2026, establishing a risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems. The guidelines cover systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users. They apply regardless of whether a model is built internally, obtained from a vendor, open-weight, or accessed through an API.

Organizations score each AI system across eight factors, including potential impact, autonomy, data sensitivity, public exposure, reversibility, sector importance, adversarial exposure, and complexity. Scores determine one of four tiers, with Tier 2 and above requiring an independent audit by a CERT-In-empanelled auditing organization; higher tiers require more extensive or frequent assessment. The article illustrates that a customer-service chatbot can move from Tier 2 to Tier 3 when it gains the ability to issue refunds, because autonomous transactions increase its autonomy, financial-data, and reversibility risks and are also a named escalation trigger.

The guidelines expect organizations to maintain a complete AI inventory, conduct threat modelling and security testing, manage third-party evidence, and reassess systems when material capabilities change. AI incidents that meet CERT-In’s reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, while CERT-In’s 2022 Directions require 180-day log retention. The article recommends that organizations identify their AI systems, assess their real capabilities, limit permissions for consequential actions, secure AI credentials, and engage an empanelled auditor early for systems in Tier 2 or above.

  • A customer-facing chatbot that only answers questions can still fall into Tier 2 because its internet exposure, use of customer data, and reliance on a partially opaque third-party model raise its score.
  • Giving a chatbot authority to issue refunds can raise its tier not only through the numerical score but also because autonomous transactions are a separate escalation trigger.
  • Organizations cannot lower a system’s inherent-risk score by pointing to safeguards already in place, because the scoring evaluates what the system can actually do before crediting controls.
  • A vendor’s refusal or inability to provide evidence about its AI model does not remove the deploying organization from audit scope; it is recorded as a limitation in the audit.
  • Auditors must independently validate an organization’s selected tier, and the higher tier applies when the auditor’s assessment exceeds the organization’s own rating.

India’s CERT-In issued guidelines for checking whether artificial-intelligence systems are safe, reliable, and properly managed. They apply to organizations in India and to companies worldwide that handle Indian data or offer AI services to Indian users, including businesses that rely on outside AI providers. Systems are rated by factors such as the sensitivity of information they use and whether they can act without a person’s approval; higher-risk systems may need regular checks by an independent approved auditor. This matters because giving an AI chatbot powers such as sending refunds can increase financial loss, data exposure, and misuse risks, while serious AI-related incidents may need to be reported within six hours.

The Take-Home Test That Runs on Your Work Laptop: Inside the AccuraSoftHire Fake Interview Campaign

A fake-job-interview campaign dubbed AccuraSoftHire used malicious npm look-alike packages, a fake camera driver, and a browser extension to infect developers with the PolinRider loader, which retrieves changing C2 addresses from Ethereum transactions and steals credentials. Organizations should search developer devices and network logs for the listed packages, artifacts, wallet-linked IPs, and immediately rotate credentials on any affected machine.
KEY POINTS
  • 01JFrog documented a fake company called AccuraSoftHire that used job listings, verified-looking recruiter profiles, coding assignments, a supposed camera driver, and a manually loaded browser extension to induce candidates to run malicious code.
  • 02The campaign’s PolinRider loader retrieves its command server address from transactions sent by Ethereum wallet 0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a, allowing the operator to change servers without updating the malicious package.
  • 03Two malicious npm packages used by the interview tasks, tailwind-lines-clamps and tailwind-lineclamp, remained available for about 211 and 169 days respectively, with npm recording more than 4,000 combined downloads in 2026.
  • 04Binance reported that an engineer ran a fake interview assignment on a work computer in September, and the attacker later used compromised systems and a deployment token to reach its internal wallet signing service before the October 29 theft.
  • 05The article advises organizations to search developer devices for the listed npm packages, automatic VS Code tasks, and the job-new-alerts browser-extension folder, then rotate all credentials from any affected machine and inspect repositories for malicious changes.

JFrog documented AccuraSoftHire, a fake hiring company that used job listings, recruiter profiles, coding assignments, a supposed camera driver, and a manually installed browser extension to persuade candidates to run malicious code. The article connects this tactic to Binance’s report that a developer ran a fake interview assignment on a work laptop before attackers ultimately reached its internal wallet signing service and stole about $6.34 billion on October 29. The article says the risk is not limited to job seekers: a compromised developer machine can expose employer credentials, deployment tokens, and source-code repositories.

The campaign’s PolinRider loader runs during a project build rather than during package installation, retrieves its server address from Ethereum wallet transactions, and downloads later stages over unencrypted HTTP on port 443. The article found that some malicious npm look-alike packages remained available for months and recorded more than 4,000 combined downloads for two of them in 2026. It recommends searching developer machines and network logs for the listed packages, automatic VS Code tasks, browser-extension artifacts, and server addresses, then rotating all credentials and checking repositories if an infection is found.

  • Blocking only newly published software packages would not have stopped this campaign’s oldest look-alike packages, because tailwind-lines-clamps and tailwind-lineclamp remained available for roughly five to seven months.
  • The malicious package code did not run when the package was installed; it ran during the project’s CSS build, meaning defenses focused only on installation-time scripts could miss it.
  • The attacker’s server-address history is publicly recoverable from Ethereum transactions, allowing defenders to search for connections to all previously used server addresses rather than only the latest one.
  • Reinstalling or wiping an infected developer laptop may not be sufficient if the malware has already inserted its loader into the developer’s code repositories, where it can run again when projects are reopened.
  • A work laptop used for an external interview can expose an employer’s credentials and internal systems even when the employee, rather than the company, is the apparent target of the recruiting scam.

A fake company called AccuraSoftHire used believable job listings and coding tests to trick software developers into running harmful programs on their work computers. The programs could steal passwords, account keys, and other access information, then spread into the developer’s work projects. This matters because a single employee taking a job interview on a work laptop can give criminals a path into an employer’s systems, as Binance says happened before its major cryptocurrency theft. The campaign also used public software-download sites and changing internet addresses, making it harder to spot and stop.

ARTEX: Attackers Adopted This AI Pentesting Tool in Three Months. Leaked Secrets Are Its Fastest Way In.

ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework, was adopted by state-linked and criminal actors within months, enabling fast, scalable intrusions that often began with exposed secrets, weak development credentials, or trusted application tokens. Organizations should rotate leaked credentials, replace long-lived CI/CD keys with short-lived OIDC tokens, remove development access from internet-facing systems, and check for compromised ARTEX Docker images.
KEY POINTS
  • 01ARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework that uses agents to plan actions, run scanning and exploit tools, and record findings against a target chosen by an operator.
  • 02Microsoft reported that AI agents searched public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials and, in at least one case, used a found secret to steal data from an Azure Key Vault within five minutes.
  • 03Threat groups including Storm-0940, VAPOR PANDA, Storm-3358, Crafty Falcon, and a South Korean criminal ring used ARTEX or related AI attack tooling against organizations in multiple countries.
  • 04A GitHub copy of ARTEX redirected installations to backdoored Docker images, which were downloaded about 9,131 times and could run commands as root before checking the login password.
  • 05The article recommends rotating exposed secrets, replacing long-lived CI/CD cloud keys with short-lived OIDC tokens, removing development credentials from internet-facing systems, and investigating ARTEX indicators such as its listed user agents and port 8787 consoles.

ARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework that assigns agents to plan attacks, scan targets, run tools, and record findings under human direction. Published on GitHub on July 26, 2026, it was reportedly adopted within months by China-linked groups, criminal crews, and a researcher whose agent accessed a WorkOS internal tool. Reports described targeting of hundreds of organizations, including financial firms, government and defense organizations, technology companies, and organizations in South Korea, Southeast Asia, India, and other countries. The original ARTEX repository was removed on October 8 after its author said the tool had been abused, but numerous copies and forks remained available.

The article’s central finding is that ARTEX agents often gain access fastest through exposed credentials, such as secrets found in public GitHub repositories, predictable development passwords deployed to production, and trusted application credentials. Microsoft reported one case in which an agent moved from searching GitHub to stealing data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes, while GitGuardian found agents could independently search code and git history for secrets even though ARTEX lacked a dedicated secret-hunting feature. A malicious ARTEX copy also redirected users to a backdoored Docker image that could run commands as root before checking a password; the image was pulled about 9,131 times. The article recommends rotating exposed secrets, using short-lived OIDC credentials in CI/CD systems, eliminating development credentials from internet-facing services, checking ARTEX installations for the malicious Docker images, and hunting for listed network indicators such as ARTEX user agents and exposed consoles on port 8787.

  • GitGuardian found that ARTEX had no built-in secret-hunting feature, yet agents in a sealed test environment independently searched code and git history and found eight of nine planted secrets, including an AWS key in history.
  • The backdoored ARTEX source copy differed from the original by only one Docker image reference, while the malicious code was contained solely in the prebuilt image, making a source-code review insufficient to detect the compromise.
  • Microsoft observed an agent correct a malformed Azure request within about 28 seconds, illustrating how automated agents can rapidly adapt without human intervention.
  • The WorkOS incident showed that an internet-exposed internal tool, a predictable development credential, no rate limits, and delayed detection allowed an agent to collect internal customer-related records without exploiting a software flaw.
  • Storm-0940 used credentials from a trusted ConnectWise Cloud Backup application to attempt access across more than 2,250 customer Microsoft 365 environments, showing how one application credential can create broad downstream exposure.

ARTEX is a tool that lets a person direct AI programs to search for weak points in computer systems and try to break in, and it was quickly used by criminal groups and China-linked groups against banks, government bodies, technology companies, and more. The fastest route was often not a sophisticated break-in but a password, cloud key, or other digital access code accidentally left online or shared between test and live systems. One copy of ARTEX was itself altered to include a hidden way for outsiders to take control of the computers running it, showing that even security tools can be dangerous when downloaded from untrusted sources. The article matters because automated tools can search and act far faster than people, turning small mistakes such as a leaked password into large-scale data theft.

Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model

AI-driven penetration-testing orchestrators such as ARTEX are rapidly proliferating, enabling attackers to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, credential abuse, and lateral movement at far greater speed and scale. Organizations should shift to an identity-gated, layered security model using WAF and bot controls, anomaly detection, schema validation, threat intelligence, credential hygiene, and micro-segmentation.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cloudflare reports that more than 50 families of AI-based penetration-testing frameworks attempted to scan its customers in the three days before publication, using thousands of IP addresses.
  • 02The ARTEX repository was removed by its creator on October 8, but Cloudflare says more than 12,000 repositories and several hundred unique forks now contain lineage from the original project.
  • 03Cloudflare observed incident-response cases in which attackers used static, non-expiring CI/CD tokens with broad cross-environment access to move from a hyperscaler environment into a customer’s Cloudflare environment.
  • 04In one investigation, Cloudflare observed ARTEX-associated activity creating Worker scripts, making more than 69 requests per minute across Cloudflare infrastructure, and issuing 400 database-dump requests in an hour.
  • 05The article recommends a six-part security model that includes WAF rate limits and anomaly detection, bot defenses, identity-gated access and micro-segmentation, API schema validation and mutual TLS, and threat intelligence.

Cloudflare reports a rapid increase in AI-based penetration-testing and exploitation orchestrators, with more than 50 framework families scanning its customers globally in three days and thousands of associated IP addresses. ARTEX, an open-source agentic penetration-testing system, was removed by its creator on October 8, but Cloudflare says its removal was followed by more than 12,000 repositories and several hundred unique forks with lineage from the original project. Daily requests associated with AI pentesting and exploitation tools have grown 30-fold since October 1.

These frameworks coordinate multiple AI agents to map targets, identify potential weaknesses, validate findings, and carry out actions in parallel. Cloudflare observed incident-response cases where attackers used static, non-expiring CI/CD tokens with broad access to move from a hyperscaler environment into a customer’s Cloudflare environment, and one ARTEX-related case involved numerous Worker scripts, more than 69 requests per minute, and 400 database-dump requests in one hour. The article recommends a six-part Modern Security Model built around WAF controls and anomaly detection, bot defenses, identity-gated access and micro-segmentation, schema validation and mutual TLS, and threat intelligence.

  • Removing the original ARTEX repository appears to have produced a “hydra effect,” as Cloudflare observed steep growth in unique instances and forks after the October 8 takedown.
  • The article highlights that the most consequential risk is not only automated scanning from the internet: stolen static CI/CD tokens can give these tools broad access to chain actions across cloud environments.
  • ARTEX activity observed in one incident included creating separately named Worker scripts for different tasks, showing how an automated framework can organize and execute multiple post-compromise actions in parallel.
  • The recommended defenses emphasize making sensitive systems unreachable without verified identity and limiting movement between environments, because credential compromise is treated as an expected condition rather than an exceptional one.

The article says that AI-powered tools for testing computer systems are spreading quickly and can also be used by attackers to search for weaknesses, break in, and move through connected systems with little human effort. Cloudflare has seen more than 50 families of these tools scanning its customers, and investigators found one case where a stolen account key was used to create many malicious programs and try to extract database information. This matters to organizations and their customers because a single leaked or overly powerful access key can let an attacker reach multiple systems much faster than before. The article recommends stronger checks at internet-facing services, tighter limits on who can access sensitive systems, and separating systems so an intruder cannot easily move further after getting in.

Glossary
*21* protocol

active-directory

also: AD, domain

A cloud-services provider that offers hosting, virtual infrastructure, and business email services.

add-ons concept

adversaries concept

A cybersecurity company providing cloud-native application security and posture management solutions.

artificial intelligence concept

asset concept

attachment concept

audit concept

audits concept

australia

authenticated concept

compromised websites concept

Confidential computing concept

Connected tools concept
Applications, services, or systems that an AI agent or workflow is allowed to use.

credit card companies concept
Businesses that issue cards, process card payments, or provide related financial services.

CSPM, or Cloud Security Posture Management, is software that checks cloud environments for risky settings and compliance problems.

customer data concept

customer information concept

Stored information about customers, such as names, account details, and contact information.
customer service concept

customer-facing services concept

cyber concept
Cyber is a broad shorthand for things related to computers, networks, and digital security.

Cyber defense is the work of protecting computers, networks, and data from digital attacks.
cyber defenses concept
Tools, practices, and systems used to protect against cyberattacks.
cyber incident concept

cyber incidents concept

cyber operations concept

cyber threat concept

cyberattacks concept

cybercriminals threat-actor

Cybersecurity concept
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, software, and data from digital attacks or misuse.
cybersecurity companies organization
Cybersecurity companies are businesses that sell services or products to help protect computers, networks, and data.
cybersecurity incident concept
A cybersecurity incident is an event that threatens the security of systems, networks, or data.

A recurring news resource that summarizes cybersecurity headlines.

data governance concept
The rules, responsibilities, and processes an organization uses to manage data safely, accurately, and legally.

data leaks concept

The processes used to collect, prepare, maintain, and deliver data for use by people and systems.

Events in which data may be lost, exposed, changed, unavailable, or handled improperly.

data theft concept
Data theft is the stealing of information from a system or service.

data-wiping malware malware

debugging technique

deception technique

defense organizations organization

detection concept

digital access concept

direct messages concept
Private, one-to-one communications sent within an online platform, like a chat or social media.

display concept

email addresses concept

exfiltrating data technique

exploited in the wild concept
Exploited in the wild means attackers are actively using a vulnerability against real targets, not just in a lab.

Information that may have been viewed, copied, or made accessible to people who were not supposed to have it.

Cyber operations intended to disrupt, damage, or interfere with another party's systems.
Offline technique
Offline password cracking means trying to guess passwords using stolen data locally rather than repeatedly logging into the target system.
OIDC protocol
OIDC stands for OpenID Connect, a protocol that helps apps confirm a user's identity during sign-in.
OIDC tokens protocol
OIDC tokens are digital proof that a user or service has authenticated through OpenID Connect.
On-premises customers concept
On-premises customers run software on their own servers or facilities instead of only in the vendor's cloud.
one-time codes concept
One-time codes are temporary numbers or passwords used to confirm a login or transaction.
Online accounts concept
Accounts used to access internet services such as email, cloud storage, social media, or websites.
online administrative services platform product
A web-based system used to provide government or administrative services to the public.
also: administrative services platform, system run by the city
online marketplaces concept
Online marketplaces are websites or platforms where buyers and sellers trade goods, services, or digital items.
online services concept
Online services are websites, apps, or internet-based systems that provide functions to users over the internet.
OODA loop concept
A decision-making cycle of observing, orienting, deciding, and acting.
open source concept
Open source means software whose source code is publicly available for people to inspect, use, modify, and share.
Open-source AI agent tool
An open-source AI agent is software whose code is publicly available and that can use artificial intelligence to perform tasks semi-independently.
open-source maintainers organization
Open-source maintainers are people who manage, review, and update publicly available software projects.
OpenAPI schema validation technique
Checking an API request against a defined format so unexpected or invalid data can be rejected.
OpenVAS tool
An open-source vulnerability scanner that checks systems for known security weaknesses.
Operating system concept
An operating system is the main software that manages a computer or phone, such as Windows, macOS, Android, or iOS.
operating system commands concept
Instructions given to an operating system, like 'dir' on Windows or 'ls' on Linux, to perform actions.
also: arbitrary operating-system commands, command output
operation-endgame
Operation Endgame is an international law-enforcement action aimed at disrupting major malware and cybercrime infrastructure.
Operator tool
An Operator is a Kubernetes automation component that manages an application by encoding operational tasks into software.
operators concept
Operators are the people or groups running a system, service, campaign, or criminal operation.
Orca organization
Orca Security is a cloud security company and platform for finding risks in cloud environments.
Orca Security organization
Orca Security is a cloud security company that helps organizations find risks across cloud environments.
Orca Sensor product
Orca Sensor is a security monitoring component that provides runtime process information and can help stop configured processes.
OtterCookie malware
OtterCookie is a malware family referenced in security reporting.
outage concept
A period when a service, website, or network is unavailable, often caused by cyberattacks like DDoS or system failures.
Outages concept
Periods when a website, service, network, or system is unavailable or not working properly.
Outlook product
Outlook is Microsoft's email and calendar application used by individuals and organizations.
Outlook.com product
Outlook.com is Microsoft's web-based email service for personal email accounts.
also: free outlook\[.]com mailbox
oversight concept
Oversight means watching over an activity or organization to make sure rules are followed and problems are caught.
OWASP organization
OWASP is a nonprofit security organization best known for publishing widely used guidance on web application risks.
OWASP GenAI Security Project organization
The OWASP GenAI Security Project is an OWASP initiative that publishes guidance about security risks in generative AI systems.
Package installation technique
Package installation means adding a reusable piece of software to a computer or project so it can be used.
Palo Alto Networks Cortex Cloud product
Palo Alto Networks Cortex Cloud is a cloud security platform for finding, preventing, investigating, and responding to threats in cloud environments.
also: Cortex Cloud
Parallels organization
A software company known for virtualization products, including Parallels Desktop.
Parliament organization
Parliament is the legislative body that the article says the Information Commissioner is directly accountable to.
Passkeys concept
Passkeys are a newer way to sign in using your device or biometrics instead of typing a password.
Passphrase concept
A password made from several words or a longer memorable phrase used to protect access.
also: a passphrase
passphrases concept
Longer passwords made from words or phrases that are used to protect an account or device.
password-spraying technique
Password spraying is when attackers try a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid quick lockouts.
Patch Tuesday concept
Patch Tuesday is Microsoft's regular monthly release day for security updates, usually the second Tuesday of each month.
also: October Patch Tuesday, November Patch Tuesday security updates
Patch Tuesday security updates concept
Patch Tuesday security updates are Microsoft’s regular monthly fixes for security flaws in its products.
patched concept
Patched means a software flaw has been fixed with an update.
patches concept
Patches are software updates that fix bugs, security flaws, or other problems.
patching concept
Applying software updates to fix security holes and bugs.
Patient information concept
Patient information is health-related personal data about people receiving medical care.
payload concept
A payload is the part of malicious code that performs the attacker’s intended action.
PCI DSS concept
PCI DSS is a security standard for organizations that store, process, or transmit payment-card data.
PCIe protocol
PCIe is a hardware connection standard used to attach devices such as graphics cards and network cards to a computer.
PDF Export concept
The process of saving or converting a document into a PDF file.
Penetration testing technique
Penetration testing is an authorized security test where people try to break into systems to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
penetration testing framework tool
A collection of tools and features used by authorized testers to find and demonstrate security weaknesses.
PentAGI tool
A self-hosted AI agent tool designed to assist with penetration testing and security tasks.
PentestGPT-Agent tool
An AI-based penetration-testing framework referenced in security reporting.
perimeter concept
A perimeter is the boundary between an organization's internal network and outside networks such as the internet.
Permission Changes concept
Changes to who is allowed to view, modify, or control a system resource or account.
persistence concept
Persistence is the ability for an attacker to keep access to a system over time.
also: establish persistence
Personal and financial information concept
Personal and financial information includes data such as names, addresses, Social Security numbers, bank details, or payment information.
personal data concept
Information relating to an identifiable individual, such as name, email, location, or financial details.
personal details concept
Personal details are information about a person, such as their name, address, phone number, or financial data, that can be misused if stolen.
Personal Health concept
Personal health information concerns an individual's medical condition, care, or wellbeing.
personal information concept
Personal information is data that can identify or describe a person, such as a name, address, phone number, or account details.
pg_dump tool
pg_dump is a PostgreSQL tool used to export or back up a database.
pg_restore tool
pg_restore is a PostgreSQL command-line tool used to restore database backups created in archive formats.
Pharmaceutical concept
Pharmaceutical refers to organizations that research, make, or distribute medicines.
PhiliKit malware
PhiliKit is a malware framework referenced in security reporting.
phishing technique
Phishing is a scam where attackers impersonate trusted people or services to steal information or make victims take unsafe actions.
phishing kit tool
A pre-packaged set of tools and templates that allows even non-technical criminals to launch phishing campaigns easily.
phishing-resistant multifactor authentication technique
Phishing-resistant multifactor authentication is a login protection method designed to resist tricking users into giving attackers access.
Phone number concept
A phone number is a personal contact detail that attackers may steal or misuse for scams and account recovery attacks.
photographs concept
Photographs are images that can contain sensitive visual details or hidden metadata such as time and location.
PHP web shells tool
PHP web shells are small scripts attackers place on a web server so they can run commands through a browser.
PHP webshells tool
Malicious PHP files placed on a web server so attackers can remotely run commands on it.
php2shell tool
php2shell is an exploit chain referenced in security reporting that is intended to obtain command execution through PHP.
